entry_sequence.action: Instead of aggressively taking liquidity, you provide the liquidity. You're placing resting limit orders in spread names ahead of large bids or offers

immediately just slamming in huge bids, only to just as quickly kick his offers out and his size out a point or two higher, and repeating it again and again before that spread compressed and the stock drifted lower

confluences.description: making the spread, especially in a liquid name
When a stock is in relative equilibrium, but thin, market participants who need urgency will cross the spread. They'll pay that offer up there and hit the bid down there.
Scalping thrives on liquidity and volatility. You need both.
by providing that liquidity, you are acting more like a market maker than a momentum trader
Often, all you need is a few high-quality opportunities where structure and order flow align.

targets.description: capture the difference between the spread as other participants are crossing and hitting the bid and paying the offer. The edge here does not come from predicting direction.

instrument_classification.instrument: US single-name stocks (in-play / liquid spread names)
instrument_classification.notes: Taught on US equities using the level-2 box (bids/offers) and time-and-sales tape and spread microstructure; not an options (Greeks/strikes) mechanic.

coaching_notes: The edge here does not come from predicting direction. It comes from understanding market microstructure.
To do this well, you must really understand market microstructure of order types, queue priority, and hidden versus visible orders.
one of the most impressive trades I've ever seen someone make was when he made hundreds of thousands of dollars in minutes during the Facebook IPO
identify a key emotional level, confirm with the tape, and execute without hesitation
There is no room for distraction, and you're interpreting real-time information and making fast, calculated decisions.
The strategy is also cognitively demanding, requiring sustained focus over the course of a long day.
The margin for error is thin, and a single large mistake can erase many small gains.
Scalping is highly execution-dependent. Minor slippage, hesitation, or routing inefficiencies can eliminate or impair your expected value.
Transaction costs matter significantly because profit targets are small relative to frequency.
The more size you do, the more slippage you face, and in turn the more your edge degrades.
you tend to need to be glued to the desk during market hours
You do not need too many trades per day... often you can fall for the trap of not being selective enough and your win rate suffers.
